summary: This unit teaches you to style hair safely and to the client's wishes: consult and analyse the hair, scalp and face shape, use blow-dryers, flat irons, curling tongs and pressing combs safely, blow-dry and heat-style straight, relaxed and natural hair, create plaits, twists, twist-outs and Bantu knots, build up-styles such as the French pleat and the chignon, and finish, advise, clean up and keep records.

blocks.p: Styling is the part of the service that the client sees and takes home. It is also where a lot of damage is done: burns from hot tools, hair broken by heat, tangles pulled out by force. This unit covers the whole styling service, from the consultation to the final mirror check. It is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees, and it builds on the shampooing, cutting and braiding units.

A good style fits the client's **hair, face, lifestyle and occasion**. A client who swims at the beach every weekend and has ten minutes each morning does not need a style that needs a flat iron every day. A stylist who listens first and styles second gives a result the client can keep.

sections.title: Working safely and hygienically with heated tools

blocks.p: Dryers, irons, tongs and pressing combs reach temperatures that burn skin in a moment and can damage hair for good. Most accidents come from a damaged cable, a wet hand, a tool left on, or a hot tool too close to the skin.

blocks.h: Hazards and how you prevent them

head: Hazard
Risk
How you prevent it
rows: A damaged plug, cable or casing
Electric shock; fire
Check every tool before use
If a cable is split or wires show, **stop using it**, label it 'Do not use' and report it to your supervisor
Never mend a cable with tape and carry on
Water near electrical tools
Electric shock
Dry your hands before touching plugs and switches
Keep tools, cables and extension cords away from basins and wet floors
Never use a tool with wet hair if it is made for dry hair
Hot plates, barrels and combs touching skin
Burns to the scalp, ears, neck, hands and forehead
Test the heat before use
Place a comb between the tong or iron and the scalp
Protect the ears and neck with your hand or a comb
Keep tools moving; never hold one on one spot
Hot tools left on a surface
Fires; burns to other people
Rest tools on a heat-proof stand
Unplug after use and let them cool before storing
Blocked dryer filter
The motor overheats; fire
Clean the air filter at the back regularly
Do not cover the air intake
Cables across the floor
Trips
Keep cables tidy and off walkways
Use a short lead or cable holder
Hairspray fumes
Irritated eyes and lungs
Spray from a distance, away from the face; ask the client to close her eyes
Ventilate the room
Dirty brushes and combs
Spread germs and scalp infections
Clean and disinfect between clients

blocks.note: If a hot tool touches the client's skin and the skin is red and sore but not broken, cool the burn **at once** under cool running water for about 10 to 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter or oil. Cover with a clean, non-stick dressing. Get medical help for a blister, broken skin or a large area, and write it in the accident book. Do not burst a blister.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Jamaica's power supply is 110 V (220 V for some heavy equipment) at 50 Hz. Check that a tool is made for the supply it is plugged into. Pressing combs that are heated on a stove or burner must have a heat-proof handle and be kept away from clothes, paper and children.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Testing the heat of a pressing comb or iron

ul: Press the heated comb or iron on a **clean white towel, tissue or paper**. If it scorches or browns the cloth, it is too hot for hair; let it cool and test again.
Never test heat by touching the metal or by wetting your finger.
Wipe off product and carbon from the comb or plates when they are cool; build-up burns and sticks to hair.
Wash your hands before each client. Use a clean gown, cape and towel for every client.
**Cleaning** (removing hair and product with detergent and water) comes first. **Disinfecting** (killing most germs with a chemical, for the contact time on the label) comes second.
After each client: remove hair from brushes and combs, wash them in warm soapy water, disinfect, rinse, dry and store covered. Never leave hair on a brush.
Do not use a comb that has dropped on the floor until it has been cleaned and disinfected.
Wipe heated tools when cool, as the maker says. Do not soak them.

If you find lice, ringworm, impetigo, sores or broken skin on the scalp, **do not style**: refer the client to a doctor or pharmacist, privately and kindly. Disinfect everything she touched and send towels for a hot wash.

sections.title: Consultation, hair analysis and choosing a style

blocks.p: The consultation is a private conversation at the mirror, before the client goes to the basin. You find out what she wants and what is possible. Many styling failures are really consultation failures.

flow: Greet the client and read her record card
Ask open questions about the style, the occasion and home care
Look at and feel the hair and scalp
Do the porosity and elasticity checks
Check for contra-indications
Look at her face and head shape
Agree the style, time and price
Record

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: The style she wants and what it is for (work, wedding, church, beach, a photograph)
Decides the technique and how long it must last. Look at any pictures.
How she looks after her hair at home, and how much time she has each morning
A style she cannot keep up will fall flat in a day.
Chemical services: relaxer, colour, bleach, perm, smoothing treatment
Treated hair is weaker and heat damages it faster.
Allergies, sensitive skin and scalp problems
To avoid products that cause a reaction.
Climate and lifestyle: humidity, swimming, exercise
Affect how long a heat style lasts.
Her budget and the time she has
Agree before you start.

head: Check
How
What it tells you for styling
rows: Curl pattern
Straight, wavy, curly or coily; look at the hair clean and product-free
Decides the method: blow-dry, silk press, twists, diffuser
Texture
Feel a single hair: fine, medium or coarse
Fine hair burns and breaks at lower heat and goes flat with heavy products; coarse hair needs more heat and tension
Density
Part the hair and see how much scalp shows
Thick hair needs more sections and time
Porosity
Slide your finger and thumb from the ends towards the roots; rough means porous
Porous hair takes in water and heat, dries fast and frizzes; use heat protectant and a gentle approach
Elasticity
Gently stretch a few damp strands; they should stretch and spring back
Poor elasticity means weak hair: avoid heat or use very low heat
Length and condition
Look at the ends and feel for dryness or damage
Damaged hair needs conditioning treatment and a trim before styling
Growth pattern
Look at the hairline, crown and nape
Cowlicks and strong growth patterns affect how a style falls

blocks.note: Natural coily hair often feels dry even when the scalp is oily, because sebum cannot travel easily down the bends of a coil. Moisturise before you apply heat, and detangle gently from the ends in sections.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Finding
What you do
rows: Open sores, cuts, scabs or crusts on the scalp
Do not style. Advise her kindly and privately to see a doctor.
Head lice, ringworm or impetigo
Do not style. Refer; disinfect everything she touched.
Burns or irritation from a recent chemical service
Do not apply heat or pull the hair; advise her to see a doctor if it is sore.
Traction alopecia or tender edges from tight styles
Style gently, with no pulling; keep heat away; advise a looser style.
Very dry, weak or broken hair
Condition first; use the lowest heat or none.

head: Face shape
What it looks like
A style that balances it
rows: Oval
A little longer than wide; forehead slightly wider than the chin
Most styles suit it
Round
As wide as it is long, with full cheeks and a soft jaw
Height on top and less width at the sides; avoid very wide, full sides
Square
A strong, wide jaw and a wide forehead
Soft waves or curls to soften the jaw; avoid severe straight lines at the jaw
Heart
A wide forehead and a narrow chin
More width at the jaw; soft fringe or side-swept styles
Long (oblong)
Much longer than wide
Width at the sides; avoid too much height
Diamond
Wide at the cheekbones, narrower at the forehead and chin
Fullness at the forehead and chin; avoid width at the cheekbones

ul: Look at the face from the front and the side. Check the head shape, the neck length and the shoulders.
Match the style to her **hair type** (a silk press will not hold on hair that reverts in the first drop of rain), her **lifestyle** and her **time**.
In Jamaica's humidity, heat-straightened hair can revert within hours of rain or sweat. A client who exercises often or swims may suit twists, braids or a low-upkeep style better.

blocks.note: Never promise a result you cannot give. Explain what her hair can and cannot do, in plain words, and agree the style and the price before you start.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Item
What it is for
Notes
rows: Blow-dryer
Dries and shapes the hair with heated air
Use a nozzle for smooth styles; a diffuser for curls; keep it moving; use the cool shot to set the shape; clean the filter.
Nozzle (concentrator)
Directs the airflow onto the section you are working on
Point it down the hair shaft, from the root to the ends.
Diffuser
Spreads the air gently, so natural curls keep their shape
For curly and coily hair.
Flat iron (straightener)
Straightens or curls hair with two heated plates
Only on dry hair. Use a heat protectant.
Curling tongs (barrel iron)
Curls dry hair round a heated barrel
A smaller barrel gives a tighter curl; a larger barrel, a looser wave.
Pressing comb (hot comb)
Straightens hair with a heated comb
Test on a white towel; keep a comb between it and the scalp.
Round brush
Gives lift and a smooth curve
Choose a size for the length and curl wanted.
Paddle brush
Smooths long, straight hair
For flat, sleek finishes.
Vent brush
Lets air through; speeds up drying
For rough drying and for short hair.
Wide-tooth comb and pick
Detangles; lifts and shapes natural hair
Start at the ends.
Tail comb and clips
Clean partings; hold sections
Use plastic clips with heat.
Hair pins, grips (bobby pins) and padding
Secure up-styles; give shape
Grips hold firmest; U-pins hold buns.

head: Product
What it does
Use and care
rows: Heat protectant
Coats the hair and reduces damage from heat tools
Apply on clean, damp or dry hair as the maker says before using a dryer, iron or tong.
Mousse and setting lotion
Gives hold and body
Light amounts on damp hair for fine hair; heavy products weigh it down.
Leave-in conditioner and styling cream
Moisture and slip; define curls and twists
Good for dry, curly and coily hair.
Gel
Strong hold and definition
Small amounts; can flake if too much.
Edge control
Smooths and holds the hairline
A little, applied gently; too much builds up.
Shine serum or oil sheen
Smooths frizz and adds shine to the finished style
Tiny amounts on fine hair; too much looks greasy.
Hairspray
Holds the finished shape
Spray from a distance, away from the face. Texture spray gives grip.
Wax and pomade
Hold and shape short or textured styles
Use sparingly.

blocks.note: Use the least amount that does the job. Always read the maker's instructions and follow the Centre's rules. Keep products off the floor, closed and labelled, and in a cool, dry place out of the sun.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A blow-dry uses heat and air to dry the hair in a shape. Done well it takes minutes off the drying time and gives smooth, bouncy, controllable hair. Done badly it gives frizz and dry ends.

Hair holds its shape through weak **hydrogen bonds**. Water and heat break them, and they re-form in the new position as the hair cools and dries. That is why you can set hair wet, then it holds as it dries. It also is why a shampoo or humid air undoes a blow-dry: the bonds break again when water gets in.

flow: Shampoo, condition and blot the hair gently; do not rub it
Detangle with a wide-tooth comb from the ends
Apply a heat protectant and any styling product
Rough-dry the hair on a medium heat until it is about 80% dry
Divide into sections and clip them
Work from the nape upwards in small sections (meshes)
Wrap each mesh round the brush with even tension
Direct the nozzle **down** the hair shaft, from the roots to the ends; move brush and dryer together
Dry each mesh fully, then use the cool shot to set the shape
Release, finish and check the balance

ul: **Blot** the hair gently with a towel: rubbing roughens the cuticle and causes tangles.
**Section** the hair so that each part is dried evenly and you keep control.
**Keep the dryer moving.** Heat held on one spot overheats the hair and the scalp.
**Point the airflow down** the hair, from the roots to the ends. This lays the cuticle flat and gives shine. Air pointed up lifts the cuticle and gives frizz.
**Cool shot** cools the hair at the end of each section and sets the shape, because the bonds re-form as the hair cools.
**Use less heat on fine, damaged or relaxed hair**, and more tension on resistant hair.
Keep the dryer a few centimetres from the hair and never touching the scalp.

head: Goal
Brush or tool
rows: Lift at the roots and a curved end
Round brush, size to the length
Smooth, sleek, straight
Paddle brush with the nozzle close
Quick, rough dry
Vent brush or fingers
Defined natural curls
Diffuser on a low setting, with the head tilted and the hair cupped
Stretched natural hair
Comb attachment with low to medium heat and heat protectant, in small sections

blocks.note: Clean the dryer's air filter often. A blocked filter makes the motor overheat, shortens the dryer's life and is a fire risk. Switch off and unplug it first.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Heat styling: irons, tongs, pressing comb and silk press

ul: **Hair must be dry.** Heat on wet hair boils the water inside the hair and can crack and blister it.
Always use a **heat protectant**.
Use the **lowest heat that works**: lower for fine, damaged, relaxed or lightened hair; higher for coarse, resistant natural hair. Stay within the maker's range and the Centre's guidance.
Work in **small sections**, so the heat goes through evenly and one pass is enough.
Do not go over the same hair many times. One or two slow passes is the rule; repeated passes burn the hair.
Place a comb between the tool and the scalp. Protect the ears, neck and forehead.
Do not use heat on hair that is already damaged or has been bleached without checking with your instructor.

head: Hair
Typical heat range for a flat iron (guide only)
rows: Fine, damaged, relaxed or bleached
Roughly 150 to 180 °C
Medium, healthy
Roughly 180 to 200 °C
Coarse, thick, resistant natural hair
Up to about 200 to 220 °C, only if the hair is healthy

blocks.note: These temperatures are a guide. Tools differ, many irons have no accurate display, and the maker's range comes first. If the hair smokes, smells burnt or goes limp, the tool is too hot: lift it off and lower the heat.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Hair dry, detangled and protected
Divide into sections and clip
Start at the nape with a thin mesh
Hold the mesh taut and glide the iron from near the root to the ends in one slow, smooth movement
Follow with a comb so the heat goes through evenly
Repeat on each mesh, then check the whole head

blocks.p: To curl with a flat iron, hold a mesh in the plates, turn the iron half a turn and slide it down, so the hair wraps round the plates and forms a wave or a curl.

flow: Hair dry and protected; section it
Place a comb between the barrel and the scalp
Hold the mesh at the ends, smoothly in the tong first, so the ends do not bend
Wind the hair up the barrel to near the root
Hold for a few seconds, as the hair needs
Release and let the curl cool before touching it

ul: To avoid **fish hooks** (bent ends), hold the ends smoothly in the tong and wind the rest up, never fold the ends back.
A **smaller barrel** gives a tighter curl; a larger barrel gives a looser wave.
Let curls cool completely before you brush or pin them; the shape sets as they cool.
A pressing comb straightens hair by heat and pressure. It is used on dry, clean, well-conditioned hair.
Test the heat on a white towel. Use a press-and-curl cream or oil as the maker or instructor says; do not overload.
Work from the nape upwards in small sections with the comb flat to the hair, holding the hair taut between the comb and the scalp with your other hand.
Wipe the comb between sections so that carbon and product do not build up.
Never put a pressing comb near the client's ears, scalp or neck; use a comb as a shield.

blocks.p: A silk press straightens natural hair smoothly with heat and no chemical, so the curl returns when the hair gets wet. Done with care it looks smooth and bouncy; done with too much heat it causes **heat damage**: hair that no longer curls.

flow: Consult: check porosity, elasticity and condition; do not press weak hair
Shampoo and condition, with a deep conditioner if needed
Detangle gently in sections, from the ends up
Apply a heat protectant to every section
Blow-dry to stretch the hair, in small sections with a comb nozzle, low to medium heat
Make sure the hair is fully dry
Iron or press each small section with one or two slow passes at the lowest heat that works
Finish lightly and wrap the hair in a satin scarf

head: Problem
Cause
Prevention
rows: Reversion (curl returns in humid weather or after rain, sweat or swimming)
Water and humidity re-break the hydrogen bonds
Advise: wrap the hair at night, avoid humid weather and sweat; use light serum
Hair stays limp or will not curl again after washing (heat damage)
Too much heat, repeated passes, or heat on weak hair
Lowest heat; heat protectant; one or two passes; skip the press if the hair is weak
Smoke, burnt smell, hair snapping
Tool too hot; hair damp
Lower the heat; make sure the hair is fully dry
Frizz at the ends
Dry ends; heat; air pointed upward
Trim; deep condition; point the dryer down the shaft

blocks.note: Humid Jamaican weather, sweat and sea water can make a heat-straightened style return to its natural curl within hours or days. Be honest with the client about how long it will last, and teach her how to protect it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Plaits, twists, rolls and natural styles

blocks.p: Many clients want styles that work with their natural hair and need little heat. These are often the most damage-free options, as long as you keep the tension low and handle the hair gently.

head: Style
What it is
Key points
rows: Plait (braid)
Three strands crossed over each other
Even tension; secure the end with an elastic.
French plait
A plait that picks up new hair into each cross as it moves down the head, lying on top of the hair
Start at the crown or hairline; keep the sections even.
Cornrow
A flat three-strand braid made close to the scalp along a parting
Straight partings; underhand braid; see the braiding unit for the full method.
Flat twist
A two-strand twist made flat on the scalp, picking up hair as it goes
Quicker and gentler than cornrows.
Two-strand twist
A section divided into two strands that are wound round each other
Even tension; finish the ends so that they do not unravel.
Twist-out
Twists taken down when fully dry to make soft, defined waves
Do not undo damp twists; they frizz.
Bantu knot
A section twisted and wound round itself into a small coil that sits on the scalp
Gives a curl when undone (a Bantu knot-out); do not wind too tightly.
Pin curls and roller set
Sections wound on rollers or pinned flat in curls on damp hair
Dry fully under a hood dryer, then cool before taking down.

blocks.h: A two-strand twist-out, step by step

flow: Shampoo, condition and detangle the hair in sections
Leave it damp, not wet, and apply a leave-in and a twisting cream to each section
Divide the hair into neat, even sections
Split each section into two strands
Twist from the root to the ends, with even tension
Seal the ends so they do not unravel
Let the twists dry **completely**; use a hood dryer if needed
Undo them gently from the ends, with a little oil on your fingers
Separate and shape the curls with your fingers; do not comb

ul: Damp twists undone too soon give frizz and a limp result. Dry hair holds its new shape.
A finger-shaped result looks softer than a combed one.
A twist-out lasts a few days to a week; wrap it at night in a satin scarf.

blocks.h: Cornrows or flat twists into an up-style

ul: A cornrow or flat-twist base keeps natural hair neat and lets you pin the ends into a bun or roll.
Plait at least the front sections from the front hairline to the crown, with clean partings and low tension, then gather the rest into a bun or roll.
Keep the tension low, especially at the edges.
Secure the finished style with grips and pins, hidden in the hair.
Work in sections, from the ends up to the roots, with a wide-tooth comb or your fingers.
Detangle when the hair is damp and has conditioner or a leave-in on it.
Do not brush dry natural hair with a bristle brush: it breaks it.
Stretch and protect the hair at night with a satin scarf or bonnet.

blocks.note: In many Jamaican families, hair has personal, cultural or religious meaning. Ask how a client wants her natural hair handled and styled, and respect her wishes.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: An up-style gathers the hair up and pins it: a bun, a roll, a French pleat or a knot at the back. Clients ask for them for weddings, graduations, church and formal evenings. They need clean, controlled hair, the right products and neat pin work.

ul: **Hair grips (bobby pins)** hold the firmest; **U-shaped pins** hold buns and rolls without flattening them; sectioning clips hold hair temporarily.
A **padding** (hair doughnut or roll) gives a bun or roll a full, even shape.
A tail comb and a wide-tooth comb for partings and backcombing; texture spray or hairspray for grip.
Pins should match the hair colour and be hidden.
Hair should be clean, dry and smooth. Very silky hair is slippery and pins slide out, so give it **grip** with a little texture spray or hairspray before you start.
Blow-dry, iron or set the hair first, as the style needs. Curled hair holds a pinned style better than flat hair.

**Backcombing (teasing)** pushes short hairs down to the root to give lift and hold. Do it lightly, in small sections near the root, and smooth the top layer over it. Brush it out gently at the end, from the ends upwards, so that you do not tear the hair.

flow: Prepare the hair: clean, smooth and, if silky, given grip
Backcomb lightly for lift at the crown, and smooth the top layer
Put a row of crossed grips up the back of the head as an anchor
Gather the hair to one side and fold it over the grips into a vertical roll, from the nape up
Secure the roll with hidden pins along its edge
Tuck in the ends, smooth stray hairs and spray lightly, away from the face
Check from every side, then show the client the back with a hand mirror
Prepare the hair and give it grip
Gather it into a low ponytail at the nape, or leave it loose
Twist or roll the hair and, if you want a full shape, wrap it round a padding
Wind the hair round the base into a knot
Pin it in place with U-pins and grips
Smooth and check

ul: Use **padding** for a full, even bun on fine hair or short hair.
Work calmly and keep the tension firm, not tight; very tight pulling hurts and breaks hair at the edges.
Check that pins are hidden and secure, and that the style does not pull the client's scalp.
Check balance: front, sides and back, in the mirror.
Check that no pins show and the hair is secure when the client turns her head.
Spray from a distance, away from the face, with the client's eyes closed.
Ask the client whether it is comfortable.

blocks.note: Hairspray is a mist of chemicals. Ask the client to close her eyes, hold the can at a distance and keep the room ventilated. Some clients dislike strong scent, so ask first.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Check the finished style from the front, sides and back, in the mirror.
Show the client the back with a hand mirror and ask whether she is happy. Make any small changes she asks for.
Apply finishing products in small amounts: serum on the ends, edge control on the edges, hairspray from a distance.
Remove the cape and loose hair from her neck and shoulders, and help her out of the chair.

head: Style
Advice
Why
rows: Blow-dry or silk press
Wrap the hair or wear a satin bonnet at night
Avoid humidity, sweat and water as much as you can
Use little heat at home, with heat protectant
Do not sleep with damp hair
Moisture and humidity break the hydrogen bonds and the style returns to its natural shape.
Curls from tongs or rollers
Do not brush the curls; separate them with your fingers
Protect them at night with a loose scarf
Brushing pulls the curl out.
Twist-out, Bantu knot-out or natural style
Moisturise lightly; wrap or pineapple the hair at night
Re-twist when the style frizzes
Keeps definition and prevents dryness.
Cornrows or flat twists
Keep the scalp clean and moisturised; dry fully after washing
Do not keep them in too long
Return if there is pain, itching or bumps
Prevents build-up, mildew and tension damage.
Up-style
Remove pins gently, one by one
Brush out from the ends upwards; do not tear backcombed hair
Prevents breakage.

ul: Recommend suitable products and say how to use them. Be honest, do not pressure her, and know the prices in JMD.
Suggest when she should return for a trim or a treatment.

flow: Unplug heated tools and let them cool on a heat-proof stand
Clean any hair and product off brushes and combs, then disinfect them
Wipe cool tools as the maker says
Put used towels and capes in the closed laundry bin
Sweep up hair and wipe the station and mirror
Close and store products
Wash your hands

head: What to record
Example
rows: Date, name, contact details
07/11/2026, Nadine Clarke, Portmore
Hair and scalp findings
Natural, coily; fine texture, medium density, high porosity; scalp healthy
Style and occasion
Silk press for a wedding
Products and tools, heat setting
Heat protectant; flat iron on a low setting; one pass
Problems or reactions
None
Aftercare given
Satin bonnet; avoid humidity; deep condition in a week
Stylist
K. Reid (trainee), checked by the instructor

blocks.note: Client records are personal information. Under Jamaica's Data Protection Act they must be kept private and secure: store cards in a locked drawer or a password-protected system, and never discuss a client's hair or health with other clients.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can check a tool's plug, cable and casing and say what to do with a damaged one.
I can test the heat of a pressing comb on a white towel and say why.
I can give first aid for a burn.
I can clean and disinfect brushes and combs and say why cleaning comes first.
I can carry out a consultation and ask open questions about the style, the occasion and home care.
I can check curl pattern, texture, density, porosity, elasticity and condition.
I can name the contra-indications to styling and say what to do about each.
I can recognise face shapes and choose a style to balance each.
I can match a style to the client's hair type, lifestyle and the humid climate.
I can explain how hydrogen bonds let hair be set, and why humidity undoes a style.
I can blow-dry in sections, pointing the airflow down the shaft and using the cool shot.
I can choose a nozzle, a diffuser and a brush for the job.
I can use a flat iron, tongs and a pressing comb safely, on dry hair with a heat protectant.
I can describe a silk press and say how to limit heat damage and reversion.
I can make plaits, French plaits, two-strand twists, a twist-out and Bantu knots.
I can prepare the hair for an up-style and make a French pleat and a chignon.
I can choose and use styling and finishing products in small amounts.
I can finish, show the client the back, give aftercare advice, clean up and fill in a record card.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step, not only the step. For example: 'I keep the dryer moving so that one spot of the hair or scalp does not overheat.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Consultation
The private conversation before a service, to agree the style and check the hair.
Curl pattern
Whether the hair is straight, wavy, curly or coily.
Texture
How thick or thin a single hair is.
Density
How many hairs grow on an area of the scalp.
Porosity
How easily the hair takes in and loses water.
Elasticity
How far a hair stretches and returns without breaking.
Hydrogen bonds
Weak bonds that break with water and heat and re-form as hair dries and cools.
Reversion
Heat-straightened hair returning to its natural curl in humid weather or when wet.
Heat protectant
A product that reduces damage from heat tools.
Nozzle (concentrator)
A blow-dryer attachment that directs the airflow.
Diffuser
A blow-dryer attachment that spreads the air gently, for curls.
Cool shot
A button that blows cool air to set the shape.
Round brush
A brush that gives lift and a smooth curve in a blow-dry.
Flat iron
A tool with two heated plates that straightens or curls hair.
Pressing comb
A heated comb used to straighten hair.
Silk press
Straightening natural hair with heat and no chemicals.
Fish hook
A bent end caused by folding the ends back on a tong or rod.
Two-strand twist
A section divided into two strands wound round each other.
Twist-out
Soft, defined waves made by undoing dry twists.
Bantu knot
A section twisted and wound into a small coil on the scalp.
French plait
A plait that picks up new hair at each cross and lies on top of the hair.
Backcombing (teasing)
Pushing short hairs down to the root to give lift and hold.
Chignon
A bun or knot worn at the back of the head.
French pleat (French roll)
A vertical roll of hair pinned up the back of the head.
Padding
A hair roll or doughnut used to give a bun or roll a full shape.
Edge control
A product that smooths and holds the hairline.
Traction alopecia
Hair loss caused by constant pulling from tight styles.
Record card
The client's record of her hair, the style, products, heat, advice and any reactions.

c1.title: A wedding up-style in Kingston
c1.text: Mrs. Hyacinth Brown, 48, asks for an elegant French pleat for her niece's wedding on Saturday. Her relaxed hair is fine and very silky, and she has had a blow-dry already. Trainee Delroy starts to pin her hair but the pins keep sliding out. He also wants to backcomb the whole head hard to make it stay. Mrs. Brown says she has a sensitive nose and dislikes strong smells.

c2.title: A silk press in the rainy season, Portmore
c2.text: Nadine Clarke, 27, has natural, coily hair that is fine in texture, dry and very porous. She wants a silk press for a wedding on Saturday afternoon in October, when it often rains. Trainee Kerone plans to press her hair while it is still slightly damp, using the highest setting on the iron and three or four passes on each section so that it is 'bone straight'. He has no heat protectant on his trolley.

c3.title: Heated tools at the Centre's salon in Mandeville
c3.text: In the Centre's salon in Mandeville, trainee Shanice finds that the cable of a flat iron has a split, with the wires showing. A trainee, Orville, is curling a client's hair close to her scalp with a hot tong and no comb, and the barrel touches her ear. A blow-dryer on the next station is very hot and smells of burning dust, and its air filter is thick with hair.

c4.title: A twist-out for church in Spanish Town
c4.text: Carla Thompson, 33, has natural medium-density, curly hair and wants a soft, defined twist-out for church on Sunday. She also swims and exercises most days and has little time for styling. Trainee Marlon washes her hair, twists it while it is soaking wet, and plans to undo the twists after only an hour under the dryer to save time.

c5.title: Choosing a style for a teacher in Mandeville
c5.text: Mrs. Beverley Francis, 40, is a primary school teacher in Mandeville. She has a square face, with a strong jaw, and fine relaxed hair, and she has only ten minutes each morning to style it. She asks for a style that suits her face and will not need a flat iron every day. She also has a patch of crusted sores on her scalp that she says she has scratched.

questions.q: Why do the pins keep sliding out of Mrs. Brown's hair?
o: Her hair is too thick for the size of the pins
Her hair is too silky and slippery to grip
Her hair is still too wet after the blow-dry
The pins are too long for this kind of style
questions.why: Very silky, fine hair gives pins nothing to hold. Give it grip with a little texture spray or hairspray, and use light backcombing at the root to make it hold.

questions.q: How should Delroy use backcombing for the French pleat?
o: Backcomb the whole head hard, to build height
Skip backcombing, because it breaks silky hair
Backcomb only the ends, so that the style holds
Backcomb lightly at the crown and smooth the top layer
questions.why: Light backcombing near the root gives lift and hold without tearing the hair. Smooth the top layer over it, and brush it out gently from the ends at the end of the day.

questions.q: Mrs. Brown dislikes strong smells. What should Delroy do when he uses hairspray?
o: Spray the whole head heavily, so that the style lasts all day
Skip the finish altogether, since she dislikes scent
Ask her, then spray lightly from a distance, eyes closed
Spray close to the scalp so the product stays on her head
questions.why: Ask first, then use a small amount, held at a distance, away from the face, with the client's eyes closed and the room ventilated. Heavy spraying irritates the eyes and nose.

questions.q: When the French pleat is finished, what is the best final step?
o: Show her the back with a hand mirror and ask if she is happy
Check only the front, since she can see that herself
Spray more hairspray over the whole head and send her to the till
Take out one pin to see how the style looks without it
questions.why: The client cannot see the back of her own style. Showing it with a hand mirror lets her check it and agree, and you can make any small changes before she leaves.

questions.q: What is the problem with pressing Nadine's hair while it is still slightly damp?
o: Damp hair will not hold the iron's heat at all
Heat on damp hair boils the water inside it and damages it
Damp hair makes the finished style curl more tightly
Damp hair is too heavy to fit between the plates
questions.why: Hair must be fully dry before a flat iron or pressing comb. Heat on damp hair turns the water to steam inside the hair, which can crack and blister it.

questions.q: What should Kerone do about the heat setting and the passes?
o: Use the highest heat and four passes for extra smoothness
Use the lowest heat that works and one or two slow passes
Use a medium heat and as many passes as she likes
Use the lowest heat but go over each section many times
questions.why: Fine, dry, porous hair burns and breaks easily. Use the lowest heat that works and one or two slow passes. Repeated passes and high heat cause heat damage.

questions.q: Kerone has no heat protectant. What is the right decision?
o: Press without one, as the hair is dry anyway
Use a little oil from the shelf instead
Use a heavy grease to protect the hair
Get a heat protectant before pressing her hair
questions.why: Heat protectant reduces damage from heat tools and should go on every section. Oil or grease can fry hair on a hot plate. Do not press without one.

questions.q: The wedding is in the rainy season. What is the most honest advice for Nadine?
o: The press will last for months, whatever the weather does
It may return to curl in rain or sweat, so wrap it and keep it dry
She should wash her hair every morning, to keep it fresh
A flat iron used three times will fix the style permanently
questions.why: Heat-straightened hair is held by weak hydrogen bonds, which water and humidity break, so the curl returns. Tell her the truth and advise wrapping the hair at night and keeping it dry.

questions.q: What should Shanice do about the flat iron with the split cable?
o: Wrap the split in tape and use it carefully
Use it only for short, quick styles for the rest of the day
Stop using it, label it and report it
Put it back on the shelf for the next stylist to decide
questions.why: A split cable with wires showing is a shock and fire risk. Take it out of use, label it 'Do not use' and report it. Taping it or passing it to someone else leaves the danger.

questions.q: Orville is curling close to the scalp. Which habit best lowers the risk of burning his client?
o: Small sections, a moving tong and a comb as a shield
Holding the tong still on each section until the curl is firm
Using the hottest setting so each curl needs less time
Curling wet hair so that the barrel stays cool
questions.why: Small sections, a moving tool and a comb between the barrel and the scalp keep the heat away from the skin. A tong held still, the hottest setting or wet hair all raise the risk of a burn or damage.

questions.q: A blister has formed on the client's ear where the barrel touched it. What should Shanice do?
o: Burst the blister and rub oil on it to dry it out
Rub the ear with ice until the pain goes away
Cool the burn, cover it and get medical help
Cover the blister with a hairstyle and carry on
questions.why: Cool the burn under cool running water, cover it with a clean, non-stick dressing, and get medical help for a blister. Do not burst it, and write it in the accident book.

questions.q: The dryer is hot and smells of burning dust. What should be done?
o: Keep using it, but on the cool setting
Turn it off, unplug it and clean the filter
Hit it gently on the side to clear the dust
Cover the back with a cloth to stop the smell
questions.why: A clogged filter makes the motor overheat, which is a fire risk. Switch off and unplug the dryer, clean the filter, and only then use it again. If it still smells, report it.

questions.q: What is wrong with Marlon twisting Carla's hair while it is soaking wet?
o: Wet hair cannot be twisted at all
Soaking wet twists take far too long to dry and may not set
Wet hair makes the twists curl far too tightly
Wet hair leaves marks on the client's clothes
questions.why: For a good twist-out the hair should be damp, not dripping, with product on it. Soaking wet twists take hours to dry and may stay damp inside, so the result is poor and can smell.

questions.q: Why should Marlon not undo the twists after only an hour?
o: Twists dry faster if they are left undone for longer
The dryer will melt the product in the twists
Twists undone while damp give frizz and a limp result
The dryer will flatten the twists if they stay in too long
questions.why: A twist-out needs completely dry twists to hold the new shape. Undoing them damp gives frizz and little definition.

questions.q: Carla swims and exercises most days. What is the best advice about her style?
o: Choose a style that needs a flat iron every morning
Choose a heat style with lots of spray, to keep it for a week
Choose a style that copes with water and is quick to redo
Choose a detailed up-style held with many pins
questions.why: A client who gets her hair wet often needs a style that copes with water and needs little time. Heat styles revert, and detailed up-styles fall apart.

questions.q: Mrs. Francis has a square face, with a strong jaw and a wide forehead. Which style helps soften it?
o: A sharp, straight cut level with the jaw
Soft waves or curls round the jaw
A slicked-back style with all the hair off the face
A heavy, straight fringe across the forehead
questions.why: Soft waves or curls soften a strong jaw. Severe straight lines at the jaw, or a hard fringe, make a square face look harder.

questions.q: What should Mrs. Francis's time limit of ten minutes tell the stylist?
o: Choose a style she can keep up at home with little or no heat
Choose a style that needs daily heat styling to hold its shape
Choose a long, detailed style that takes an hour to put in
Choose a style that only a stylist can refresh for her
questions.why: A style must suit the client's lifestyle and time. A simple, low-upkeep shape cut well or a simple set that she can do in minutes is better than a style she cannot keep up.

questions.q: What should the stylist do about the crusted sores on Mrs. Francis's scalp?
o: Style around them with the dryer on a cool setting
Do not style, and tactfully advise her to see a doctor
Put a little styling oil on the sores to help them heal
Cover the sores with a hairstyle that hides them
questions.why: Crusted or broken skin is a contra-indication, because heat, product and handling can hurt her scalp and spread infection. Advise her tactfully, in private, to see a doctor, and write it on the record card.

questions.q: A client wants a tighter curl with curling tongs. What should you change?
o: Use a smaller barrel
Use a larger barrel
Use a higher heat setting
Use more hairspray before curling
questions.why: The barrel size decides the size of the curl: a smaller barrel gives a tighter curl and a larger barrel a looser wave. Higher heat only risks damage.

questions.q: After three passes with the iron, a client's hair smells burnt and snaps when stretched. What is the most likely cause?
o: The iron was too cool, so it needed more passes
Too much heat and too many passes on the same hair
The hair was too clean for the iron to glide
The plates were too wide for the section
questions.why: Burnt smell and snapping show the hair has been overheated. One or two slow passes at the lowest heat that works is the rule; extra passes at high heat burn the hair.
